justification:
Technical round 1 for /oop-design/interfaces-vs-abstract-classes/. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/oop-design/interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md` from PowerShell, run three times: PASS, blocks=31, executed=20, identical result each time, no flakiness. All 20 `run` blocks (including the 7 expected-compile-error blocks: CS0122, CS1061, CS8705x2, CS0525, CS0526, CS0315, CS0535x2) and both exercise solutions were read for correctness and idiom; found no bugs (Fraction's GCD/zero-denominator guard, ThrottledNotifier's counter and Reset exercise, and the batch-sum arithmetic 1/4+1/2+1/8=7/8 all check out by hand).

Highest-priority check, done independently rather than trusted: the default-interface-member accessibility claim. I wrote my own file-based C# programs (not copied from the article) on .NET 10.0.401 and reflected on an interface with an unmarked default-bodied method: `IsPublic=True`, matching a bodyless member and differing from an explicitly-`private` sibling (`IsPublic=False, IsPrivate=True`) declared in the same interface. I separately confirmed by direct usage that outside code can call the unmarked default-bodied member through the interface type with no cast and no accessibility error, exactly as public bodyless members behave. I then fetched the C# language specification's interfaces chapter myself (learn.microsoft.com/.../language-specification/interfaces) and found the exact sentence the article quotes, verbatim: "All interface members implicitly have public access; however, an explicit access modifier ([§7.5.2]) is permitted except on static constructors." This is unqualified by whether the member has a body. My independently-compiled evidence and the formal spec agree, and agree with the article: **default interface members are public by default** unless marked otherwise. Notably, in the course of this check I also fetched learn.microsoft.com/.../keywords/interface (the article's source [2]) and found it explicitly states the opposite for bodied members: "Interface members with a default implementation are `private` by default if you don't specify an access modifier" -- this MS Learn tutorial page is itself wrong, contradicted by both the formal spec and actual compiler behavior on .NET 10. The article's own citations are careful about this: it cites the language spec (source [6]) and the fundamentals page's unqualified "public by default" (source [3]) for the accessibility claim, and never relies on or repeats the interface-keyword page's incorrect "private by default" line for bodied members, even though that same page is correctly cited elsewhere (DIM existence, static abstract members, versioning). The writer's claimed correction is verified correct; had it been backwards, that would have been the capping error this review was told to watch for. It is not.

Diamond-problem investigation, compiled independently with fresh type/variable names (not the article's `INotifier`/`IPersistable`/`IAuditable` identifiers) to avoid trivially re-running the same code: (a) two unrelated interfaces with same-name/signature defaults and no common ancestor -> compiles cleanly, both defaults reachable only through their own interface type, no ambiguity -- confirmed. (b) two interfaces both deriving from a shared ancestor, both re-implementing the ancestor's member with explicit interface syntax -> genuinely fails, `CS8705: Interface member 'IShared.Tag()' does not have a most specific implementation` -- confirmed. (c) one of the two competing interfaces derives from the other -> the more-derived interface's override wins automatically with no error -- confirmed. The language spec's §19.4.10 text I fetched matches the article's citations precisely: "if `I2` and `I3` are interfaces implemented by `T` and `I3` derives from `I2` either directly or indirectly, `I3.M` is a more specific implementation than `I2.M`", and "Otherwise, neither `I2.M` nor `I3.M` are more specific and an error occurs" -- both quoted/paraphrased accurately, and the spec's own worked example (`IA`/`IB`/`IC`/class `C`/class `D`) is structurally the same shape the article builds.

CS0525 (field in interface) and CS0526 (instance constructor in interface) reproduced independently with fresh code -- both fire exactly as claimed. The static abstract members section was independently rebuilt with fresh names (`ICombinable<TSelf>`/`Money` in place of `IAddable<TSelf>`/`Fraction`) and produces the correct summed value; the `IMultipliable<int>`-style CS0315 rejection of `int` was reproduced independently (`int` cannot satisfy `where T : ICombinable<T>` because `int` doesn't and can't implement a user-defined interface) with the exact diagnostic; the `INumber<T>` pivot was reproduced independently for both `int` and `double` sequences and sums correctly. CS0535 versioning before/after reproduced independently (adding a bodyless member breaks existing implementers; giving it a body fixes them without touching them).

All six cited sources are real, current Microsoft Learn pages, fetched and read directly: the default-interface-methods-versions tutorial's "already released and used by innumerable clients" line is quoted near-verbatim from the live page; the abstract-keyword page confirms fields, constructors, and non-instantiability for abstract classes and confirms static abstract/virtual members are interface-only, never legal on a class (even an abstract one), matching the capability table; the generic-math page confirms the INumber<T>/IAdditionOperators motivation and the pre-C#-11 gap the article describes; the language-spec quotes are verbatim as detailed above. Compared against two real published treatments of this topic (Microsoft's own interface-keyword page, and tutorialsteacher.com's C# interfaces tutorial): neither attempts the unrelated-vs-shared-ancestor diamond distinction or the automatic-tie-break case at all, tutorialsteacher states the public-by-default rule without engaging the DIM nuance Microsoft's own page gets wrong, and neither verifies its own accessibility claims against a reflected member or the spec text the way this article does. That differentiation, combined with the verified-correct correction of a live Microsoft documentation error, is real, checkable value-add, not filler.

Not a 10: the article never states in its own prose that Microsoft's interface-keyword tutorial page itself gets this wrong ("private by default" for bodied members) -- it simply avoids citing that page for the claim and sources the correct spec text instead. An explicit sentence naming and correcting that documentation error would be a stronger, more differentiated reader payoff than silently routing around it, and is the only material improvement I found after a full independent pass. No factual error, incorrect claim, or code that fails to run was found anywhere in the article.

issues.location: Default interface members section, the paragraph beginning "No modifier was written on `Describe`"
issues.problem: The article correctly sources the public-by-default claim to the language spec and avoids relying on Microsoft's own interface-keyword tutorial page (source [2]) for that specific point -- and that page is independently confirmed (by this reviewer, via a live fetch) to say the opposite ("private by default" for bodied members) and to be wrong when checked against the spec and actual compiler behavior. The article never says so explicitly; a reader who goes to check source [2] for this claim will find it contradicts what the article says, with no warning.
issues.fixLooksLike: One sentence naming the discrepancy directly, e.g. "Microsoft's own interface-keyword reference currently states the opposite for bodied members ('private by default'); the specification and the compiler's own output above do not agree with it." This turns a silent routing-around into an explicit, differentiated correction, which is stronger AdSense value-add and a better reader outcome than omission.
